name: Maternal and foetal malnutrition in South Asia one of the highest in the world

content.text: In her keynote address, Dr Ellen G. Barclay from UNICEF (ROSA), presented an overview of maternal malnutrition. She noted that while a lot of research had been conducted in the field of child malnutrition, there is scarce data available on women's nutritional status in South Asia. She emphasised that it was crucial to develop strategies and tools, and build parameters within which to assess and analyse the problem in order to come up with an action plan. This would include, for example, desegregating data such as gender, geographical area, age, etc. to facilitate assessment. She also pointed out that the prevalence of other co-existing illnesses such as tuberculosis often diminished the focus on maternal malnutrition.

Dr Barclay also highlighted the fact that childhood malnutrition could never be conquered unless a woman's inherent right to nutrition was assured. A mother must be able to provide proper care for herself before she can give the best to her child. In South Asia, not only is female malnutrition a result of inadequate food intake due to poverty, but also inadequate access to food within the household due to their subordinate status. Dr Barclay concluded that it was time to inform, educate and challenge existing conventions.

An important result of maternal malnutrition is low birth weight. If a mother is not fed the right foods in the proper quantities, her child will be affected. Dr Zulfikar A. Bhutta, Professor of Pediatrics and Child Health at AKU, presented an overview of low birth weight in South Asia. Quoting from a variety of sources, he underlined the difficulty in adequately defining the problem. However, irrespective of differences in definition throughout the region, Dr Bhutta suggested that at least half a million low birth weight infants are born in Pakistan each year. These infants have a disproportionately high risk of dying during childbirth or in the first few weeks oflife. He also noted that it was a well established fact that these infants have a higher proclivity to life threatening illnesses during early childhood, such as respiratory infections and diarrhoea. Finally, he stated that many of the long term effects of low birth weight such as increased risk of diabetes, hypertension and premature coronary artery disease are very poorly understood in the South Asian context.

The two- day workshop will be followed on 30 October by an international seminar" Women and Nutrition in South Asia: Issues and Strategies for Change". The key note address will be delivered by Professor Robert E. Black, Johns Hopkins, USA and national and international academicians will attend.

content.title: Maternal and foetal malnutrition in South Asia one of the highest in the world
content.author: volunteer.pa
content.description: A two- day international workshop on "Maternal and Foetal Malnutrition and Human Development in South Asia" is being held at The Aga Khan University (AKU) on October 28 and 29, 1999. It will address issues such as maternal malnutrition and resultant low birth weight in South Asia and formulate a coherent, practical and effective policy for public health planners throughout the region.
